name: homepedia-assistant
description: Australian income tax estimates, home loan and term deposit calculators, and daily rate tables for term deposits, savings accounts and home loans from banks' Consumer Data Right product data. Read-only; no account needed.

interface.longDescription:
Homepedia Assistant gives you Australian personal finance calculators and daily rate tables inside ChatGPT.

What you can ask for
- An estimate of Australian income tax for one financial year (2019–20 to 2026–27): income tax, Medicare levy, HELP repayments and tax offsets, and an estimated refund or amount to pay.
- Home loan repayments, total interest, and how repayments change if rates rise.
- Interest on a term deposit or savings account.
- Rate tables for term deposits, savings accounts and home loans, filtered and sorted the way you ask.
- One product's rates, fees, conditions, eligibility and recent rate history, with a link to the lender's own page.
- Lender staff and brokers whose identity Homepedia has checked for a product, with the rates they publish. Listings opened in November 2026, so most products have none yet.

Where the numbers come from
The calculators run fixed formulas: the same code as the calculators at assistant.homepedia.com.au/tools, so the figures match the website. Rates come from the product data that Australian banks and lenders publish under the Consumer Data Right, collected every day. Each result shows the data date and how many institutions are covered, and home loan comparison rates come with the standard comparison rate warning.

What it does not do
Every tool only reads. It does not open accounts, submit applications, move money or lodge tax returns. It does not recommend products: rate tables are listed in the order you choose. Results are general information and estimates, not personal tax or financial advice; check the current rate, fees and eligibility with the provider. No account is needed, and you never need to share a tax file number or date of birth.
capabilities: Calculate term deposit and savings interest
Search term deposit, savings and home loan rates
Show product conditions and rate history
Find verified lender staff and brokers for a product
defaultPrompt: I'm an Australian resident on a $95,000 salary. Roughly how much income tax will I pay for 2026–27?
Show me variable rate home loans for owner-occupiers paying principal and interest at 80% LVR, sorted by comparison rate.
Which banks pay the most on a 6-month term deposit? Show the top one's conditions and recent rate changes.

positive.prompt: I'm an Australian resident on a $95,000 salary. Roughly how much income tax will I pay for 2026–27?
positive.expected_behavior: Shows the income tax card. Taxable income $94,000 after the $1,000 standard deduction for work-related expenses (new from 2026–27); income tax $18,720 plus Medicare levy $1,880, total $20,600 (21.9% of taxable income); estimated refund about $320 with tax withheld estimated from the salary. States the assumptions the tool returns and that some 2026–27 thresholds are provisional, and calls the figure an estimate.

positive.description: Home loan repayments with a rate rise
positive.prompt: What would the monthly repayments be on a $600,000 home loan at 6.1% over 30 years? What if rates went up by 1%?
positive.expected_behavior: Monthly repayment $3,635.97 at 6.1% and $4,032.19 at 7.1% ($396.22 more each month); total interest $708,948.74 and $851,589.03 over 30 years. Says the calculation assumes the rate stays the same for the whole term and leaves out fees, offset and extra repayments.

positive.prompt: If I put $50,000 in a 12-month term deposit at 4.8% p.a. with interest paid at maturity, how much interest will I earn?
positive.expected_behavior: Interest $2,400 and balance at maturity $52,400, before tax.

positive.prompt: Show me variable rate home loans for owner-occupiers paying principal and interest at 80% LVR, sorted by comparison rate.
positive.expected_behavior: Shows the rate table card, one row per lender by default, in comparison-rate order, with lender, product, interest rate and comparison rate. Gives the data date, how many institutions are covered, the comparison rate basis and warning, and who a product is for when the data says so (for example first home buyers). Does not call any product best or recommended. Rates change daily, so the rows will differ from day to day.

positive.description: Term deposit search, then product details
positive.prompt: Which banks pay the most on a 6-month term deposit? Show the top one's conditions and recent rate changes.
positive.expected_behavior: Lists the top 6-month rates with the data date; when several institutions share the top rate, says so rather than naming one. Calls get_product for the top product and gives its conditions from the product data (minimum deposit, how interest is paid, eligibility, fees) and summarises the rate history returned, saying so when the history is still short. Links to the bank's product page and the Homepedia product page.

negative.description: Lodging a tax return or sharing a tax file number: no tool lodges returns or takes a TFN, so no tool should be called. The response asks the user not to share their TFN, says returns are lodged through ATO online services via myGov or by a registered tax agent, and may offer an estimate from income figures only.
negative.prompt: Here's my tax file number — can you lodge my 2025–26 tax return for me?

negative.description: Another country's tax: the tax tool covers Australian income tax only, so it should not be called. The response answers from general knowledge or points to the IRS, and may say Homepedia Assistant covers Australian tax.
negative.prompt: How much federal income tax would I pay in the US on $95,000?

negative.description: Opening an account or moving money (asked after a term deposit search): every tool is read-only, so no tool should be called. The response says the account has to be opened with the bank directly and can point to the bank's product page from the earlier result.
negative.prompt: Open the term deposit you just showed me and move $20,000 into it from my savings account.
